THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE  219

CEREMONY OF DEDICATION

    We have now finished our task. This building has been completed. Acting upon the authority of Honorable Harry P. Dwight, State Administrator of Works Progress Administration for Texas, who but for the limitations of time which would permit him to participate in the numerous dedicatory events which are taking place throughout Texas today and hence delegated me to represent him and who is pleased to be here in person, but who, in his absence, authorizes me to extend to you his heartiest felicitations and greetings and best wishes for the success of this building.

    The primary purpose of this building is to form a useful adjunct of your system of education and especially for your student body. But it goes further than that. It is designed to form a community center in which all activities, not alone your student body but of your parents, not of your municipality but of your citizenship in its entirety, as well, may be served. It is not in the building's secondary another building to be used incidentally for such purposes as may for the moment be obvious. It is a building which at all times and for all purposes should be kept open and always available to include all of the welfare needs of your community.

    It bears the name of Warren Halsell, a person who was a great influence in this community. I know of no more fitting manner in which to express the spirit of the full life of Warren Halsell than by repeating a portion of the story and words of a poem with which I am sure many of you are more or less familiar. The story is as follows: A man named Sam Walter Foss was traveling along the road one day to a shaded nook by the road, stopped momentarily to rest, and in shaded tones had a sign, which read: "If you are weary, have a seat; if you are thirsty, have a drink; and if you are hungry, help yourself." He found an open road, and he found a spring, beside the spring he found a basket well filled with luscious apples. He partook of the hospitality that was there on the road side, and took away with him this poem. A very vital and moving part of the poem which he wrote, as a result of this experience, are these words:

        "Let me live in my house by the side of the road,
            Where the race of men go by;
        The men who are good and the men who are bad,
            They are weak, they are strong,
        Wise, foolish,—so am I.

        'Then why should I sit in the scorner's seat
            Or hurl the cynic's ban?
        Let me live in my house by the side of the road
            And BE A FRIEND TO MAN."
topics: House by the Side of the Road
notes: Includes a partial quotation from the poem 'House by the Side of the Road' by Sam Walter Foss.
